new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the radical (stem-initial) syllable, i.e. the first syllable after the noun-class/verbal prefix; cues are the full seven-vowel contrast being licensed only there and greater duration of the radical vowel (li-Wanji radical [u] 106 ms vs prefixal [u] 70 ms). Li-Wanji does not reduce or drop final vowels (unlike some other B50 lects). The language is otherwise tonal (H vs L lexical tones, downstep; an upstepped H under emphasis docks on the word-initial, i.e. prefix, syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Under emphasis ('insistent' forms) lengthening affects primarily the initial (prefix) syllable and secondarily the final syllable, the stressed radical syllable least (Table 2, p. 181) — this is emphatic prominence, not secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement; notes only that final-vowel reduction found elsewhere in B50 does not occur in li-Duma or li-Wanji, and that in LL stems an upstepped H spreads over prefix+radical vowels in li-Wanji but only the radical vowel in li-Duma.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is framed for 'B50 Bantu' generally and instantiated with instrumental measurements on li-Wanji words (mú-kárí, mú-lúmì, mú-bɔ̀ːŋgɔ́, mú-βéɣà) uttered in the presentative construction; domain is the (prefixed) word, stress on stem-initial syllable. Li-Wanji data supplied by Médard Mouélé, native speaker. Supporting first-hand hint: Hombert & Mouélé 1988: 193 refer in passing to 'l'accent sur la première syllabe du thème' for Wanzi; all other accessible descriptions (Hombert & Mouélé 1988, Mouélé 1993, Niama Niama 2021) describe only the two-tone system.
new_statements.identity_note: Puech 1990 treats li-Duma (B51, Glottolog duma1253) and li-Wanji as 'two dialects of a western Bantu language spoken around Lastoursville'; the stress statement is framed for B50 generally but the duration evidence quoted is measured on li-Wanji (= Liwanzi/Wandji, B501, wand1266) words supplied by native speaker Médard Mouélé (whose own work describes 'wanzi-est', the Moanda variety). Hombert & Mouélé 1988 and Mouélé 1993 describe the same Liwanzi. No separate glottocodes exist for East (Moanda) vs West (Lastoursville) Wanzi.

sources.note: Synchronic section (pp. 184-186) gives tone system (2 tonemes H/L; four Proto-Bantu tone patterns preserved even in isolation), vowels, consonants; no stress rule. Only a passing diachronic remark p. 193: transfer of a fortis/lenis distinction from prefix to C1 'aurait pu être favorisé par le rôle grandissant joué par l'accent sur la première syllabe du thème' (presupposes stem-initial accent).

sources.note: Sec. 1.1.5 Liwanzi (B501), pp. 67-73: phonetic/phonological sketch after Hombert & Mouélé 1988 and Mouélé 1997 (14 vowels with length contrast, consonants, 2 tonemes H/B, syllable types); no word-stress statement. Pp. 271-272, 296: speculates that in B50 the H/L contrast survives only in T1 (stem-initial) position, 'laissent soupçonner une évolution vers un processus accentuel' (citing Philippson 1991, Dodo-Bounguendza 2010) — no statement of stress position for Liwanzi.

sources.note: Section 2.1 'Les tons': li-wanzi has two level tonemes (H, B) combining into falling/rising; ideophones add extra contour tones on long vowels. Nothing on stress/accent.
